prompt: Let $h(x) = \int_0^{x^2} \cos t \, dt$. Which expression equals $h'(x)$?
hint: The upper limit is $x^2$, not $x$. That makes $h$ a composition, $h(x) = G(x^2)$ where $G(u) = \int_0^u \cos t \, dt$, so the chain rule is needed.

hints.text: The upper limit is $x^2$, not $x$. That makes $h$ a composition, $h(x) = G(x^2)$ where $G(u) = \int_0^u \cos t \, dt$, so the chain rule is needed.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up: if $G(u) = \int_0^u \cos t \, dt$, then by the FTC $G'(u) = \cos u$. Now $h(x) = G(x^2)$, so $h'(x) = G'(x^2) \cdot (x^2)'$.
The outside piece is $G'(x^2) = \cos(x^2)$ and the derivative of the upper limit is $(x^2)' = 2x$. Multiply these two pieces together.
The derivative is $h'(x) = 2x \cos(x^2)$, which is choice A.

explanation: Write $h(x) = G(u)$ with $u = x^2$ and $G(u) = \int_0^u \cos t \, dt$. By the FTC, $G'(u) = \cos u$.
The chain rule multiplies by the derivative of the upper limit: $h'(x) = G'(u) \cdot \frac{du}{dx} = \cos(x^2) \cdot 2x$.
That is choice A. Choice B forgets the chain rule factor, and C and D confuse "derivative of the integral" with actually integrating $\cos$ to get $\sin$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Integrate first, then differentiate
steps: Same answer. This route works here because $\cos$ has a simple antiderivative; the FTC-plus-chain-rule route works even when it does not.
